title: The Korean retreat season
hookLine: twice a year Korean monks and nuns sit for three months without leaving

cards: On a set day, the gates of a Korean mountain monastery close behind a hall of monks, or nuns, their cushions laid out in rows. They won't walk out again for three months. No trips to town, no visits home.

Sitting, walking, eating, sleeping, sitting again, each carrying a single question. When the season ends, the gates open, and some shoulder a pack and walk off to another monastery for the months between.
Twice a year, this happens. Today: the Korean retreat season.

teach.h: A RULE FOR THE RAINY SEASON.
teach.b: First, the root. The old monastic rules, the Vinaya, tell how the rainy-season retreat began.

In the Vinaya's story, people complained that wandering monks were tramping through the fields in the rains, crushing young plants and small creatures. So the Buddha told the monks to stay in one place for the rains.
A practical rule for a muddy road became a lasting rhythm of monastic life. Second, the Korean shape.
The season comes twice, summer and winter, each about three months. The word is angeo, dwelling in peace. The start is gyeolje, a binding; the end is haeje, an untying.
In the months between, monks and nuns travel, visit teachers, or move to a new hall. Third, the days.
Seon halls keep long sitting periods from before dawn into the night, with walking between, and yesterday's hwadu is the work: one question, held all season.
Some halls keep an even stricter retreat for those who want it.
Fourth, who it's for. The hall belongs to the monks and nuns who sit it, but some Korean temples open shorter retreats for laypeople, a weekend or a few days, so anyone can taste the season.
The closed gates are part of a bigger rhythm: going in, coming out, going in again.

how: In Korean Seon monasteries, monks and nuns enter the summer and winter retreats (angeo) together, staying inside the monastery for the season and following a schedule of long sitting periods with a hwadu; some temples also hold short retreats open to laypeople.

tell the people to fence their fields.
games.why: he sets the rainy-season residence. a practical rule for a muddy season became a lasting rhythm of monastic life.

practice: Picture, gently, a retreat of your own someday: a quiet day, a weekend at a temple, a morning with the phone in a drawer. What would you leave at the gate, and what one question might you carry in?
Hold the plan lightly, like a seed, then let it go and sit in this small retreat you're already in.

wordCard.voice: The Korean retreat season. Angeo: twice a year, summer and winter, monks and nuns stay inside the monastery for about three months of intensive Seon practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Korean: angeo, the retreat season, written in Chinese characters as 安居, 'peaceful dwelling'; Pali vassa, the rains.

carryVoice: Your line: three months in. Every season starts with a gate closing. Back tomorrow, same hill.
